title: Publication and genre
short: First printed in 1680 in a volume of poems attributed to Rochester, then in Behn's own Poems upon Several Occasions (1684); an 'imperfect enjoyment' poem.
body: The 'imperfect enjoyment' was a Restoration genre about male impotence at the moment of seduction, going back to Ovid's Amores 3.7 and represented by Rochester's 'The Imperfect Enjoyment', printed in the same 1680 volume. Behn adapted part of the French poem 'L'occasion perdue recouverte', attributed to Jean Benech de Cantenac. Her version is distinguished by attention to the woman's experience: Cloris's confusion and disappointment, rather than the man's humiliation alone, become the subject. Jessica Munns (in Aphra Behn Studies, ed. Janet Todd, 1996) notes how unusual its focus on female sexual experience was for its time.

title: Lysander and Cloris
short: Conventional pastoral names; the shepherd and the nymph place the poem's frankness inside an artificial classical setting.
body: Lysander (from Greek) and Cloris (Chloris, a Greek goddess of flowers) are stock names from pastoral poetry and romance. The pastoral setting (thicket, moss, shepherdess gathering fern) creates a distance that allows erotic frankness, a strategy Behn uses in many poems. Lysander 'surprises' Cloris, i.e. comes upon her unexpectedly or takes her unawares; the verb sets up the poem's uneasy blend of seduction and force.

title: Stanza form
short: Ten-line stanzas of mainly eight-syllable lines rhyming abbacdcdee, each closing on a ten-syllable line.
body: Each stanza closes with a couplet whose final line is lengthened (for example 'But what from Cloris Brighter Eyes was hurld'), giving a falling cadence. The brisk tetrameter suits narrative and erotic suspense, and the lengthened last lines allow ironic summaries. The scheme is maintained throughout the fourteen stanzas, and the regularity of the form contrasts comically with the irregularity of the event it narrates.

sources.cite: The Works of Aphra Behn, ed. Janet Todd, vol. 1: Poetry (Pickering & Chatto, 1992), notes to 'The Disappointment'

anchor: The gilded Planet of the Day
title: The sun's chariot
short: A mock-epic periphrasis for sunset: the sun (Phoebus Apollo) drives his fiery chariot down to the sea.
body: In classical myth the sun-god drives a fiery chariot across the sky and descends into Ocean at evening. The elevated diction ('gilded Planet', 'gay Chariot drawn by Fire') provides the setting, and when only 'Cloris Brighter Eyes' give light the hyperbole flatters the heroine in the Petrarchan way. The Apollo allusion anticipates the later comparison of Cloris to Daphne fleeing 'the Delphick God'.

anchor: Permits his Force, yet gently strove
title: Consent and force
short: Cloris 'permits his Force' while gently resisting: the convention of feigned resistance, which modern readers find troubling.
body: Restoration erotic verse often presents a woman's resistance as a sign of modesty that conceals desire, and the lines follow that convention: 'Silent as yielding Maids Consent', her hands meet his bosom 'not to put him back'. Her spoken protest in the third stanza ('Cease, Cease') complicates this, and the poem invites debate about whether Behn reproduces the male fantasy of the willing victim or exposes its contradictions by entering the woman's perspective. Some commentators note how honour and shame are treated as forces acting on Cloris from outside.

title: Love against shame
short: Cloris's eyes show love and shame in conflict; the struggle between desire and honour runs through her speech.
body: Shame and honour were the terms in which a woman's sexual reputation was discussed. Cloris pleads that her 'Dearer Honour' she 'cannot, must not give' and offers her life instead, the conventional heroic choice. The poem later notes that she is 'Abandon'd by her Pride and Shame' (st. 7), suggesting desire's victory, and finally shame returns in her blushes at the discovery of Lysander's failure.

anchor: His daring Hand that Altar seiz
title: Religious metaphors for the body
short: Cloris's sex is figured as an altar, a throne, a paradise and a fountain, a sacred blazon pushed to the point of wit.
body: The blazon was the poetic catalogue of a woman's body; here the most intimate part receives sacred and royal titles ('Altar', 'Awful Throne', 'Paradice'). 'Awful' means awe-inspiring. The religious diction of sacrifice is developed in the following stanzas, where Lysander lies 'Unable to perform the Sacrifice'. The metaphors combine mock-solemnity with a genuinely elevated idea of sexual pleasure as giving 'the Universal World Repose'.

title: The failed sacrifice
short: Lysander, 'o'er-Ravish'd', cannot perform the rite: the climax of the religious metaphor is impotence.
body: Cloris offers her 'Virgin-Innocence' as 'A Victim to Loves Sacred Flame', the language of ritual sacrifice, but the priest fails. 'O'er-Ravish'd' means carried away by excessive rapture, the irony being that excess of desire produces incapacity. The paradox 'Pleasure which too much Love destroys' (st. 8) is the genre's standard explanation, found in Ovid and Rochester. Behn's word 'Ravish'd' also glances back at the force Lysander used, so the vocabulary of violence returns as the vocabulary of his failure.

title: Periphrasis for the penis
short: The male organ is named only by circumlocution, as 'Nature's Support', a mock-heroic periphrasis.
body: The stanza describes the failure in elevated, scientific and military language: 'slack'ned Nerves', 'fleeting Vigor', 'Motion' (a philosophical term borrowed from contemporary mechanical philosophy). 'Essay'd' means tried. The ironic line 'Excess of Love his Love betray'd' summarises the paradox, and 'The Insensible fell weeping in his Hand' makes the failure explicit in a deliberately grotesque image. Here 'Insensible' is a noun: the organ that has lost all feeling.

title: Priapus
short: Priapus, the Greek god of fertility and gardens, represented with a huge phallus; 'Fabulous' means legendary, with a pun on fable.
body: Priapus was worshipped as a guardian of gardens and flocks and was proverbial for sexual potency; Latin Priapea poems are spoken by him. Behn's 'Fabulous', meaning legendary but also mythical and false, mocks the gap between the 'Potent God, as Poets feign' and the reality Cloris discovers. The comic irony is that the classical god of virility here represents failure.

title: The snake in the grass
short: The shepherdess who touches a hidden snake recalls Virgil's 'latet anguis in herba' (Eclogues 3.93).
body: Virgil's shepherd warns the boys gathering flowers and strawberries that 'a cold snake lies hidden in the grass' (Eclogues 3.92-93). Behn's simile turns a pastoral commonplace into a sexual joke: Cloris draws back her hand as quickly as a girl gathering fern would from a snake, but because the 'God of her Desires' is 'Cold as Flow'rs bath'd in the Morning Dew'. The comparison combines comedy with the poem's sympathy for Cloris's shock.

anchor: Or Daphne from the Delphick God
title: Daphne and Apollo
short: Cloris flees like Daphne running from Apollo in Ovid's Metamorphoses, though her motive is disappointment, not chastity.
body: In Metamorphoses 1, the nymph Daphne flees Apollo, the god of Delphi, and is turned into a laurel. The allusion is ironic: Daphne flees a pursuing god's desire, whereas Cloris flees the absence of it. The wind that reveals her body as she runs ('Discover'd in the Flying Maid') comes directly from Ovid's description of Daphne's flight, where the breeze bares her limbs.

title: Venus and Adonis
short: Cloris's flight is compared to Venus hurrying to the dying Adonis, killed by a boar.
body: In Metamorphoses 10, Venus, hearing the groans of Adonis gored by a boar, hurries back to find him dead. The comparison makes Lysander's failure a kind of death and lends Cloris's flight the dignity of mythological grief, with mock-heroic exaggeration. 'Love' here means the lover. Shakespeare's Venus and Adonis was a popular treatment of the same story. The Venus simile ends the narrative of Cloris; the final stanza turns to the narrator and to Lysander.

title: The narrator's voice
short: The narrator suddenly speaks as 'I', claiming that only she can imagine the nymph's resentment: an assertion of female perspective.
body: Only in the last stanza does the narrator reveal a sympathy with Cloris that critics read as the voice of a woman poet. Male poets in the genre (Ovid, Rochester) concentrate on the man's shame; Behn claims special insight into the woman's 'Resentments', while Lysander's soul, she says, only the powers who 'sway'd his Destiny' can guess. Munns and others argue that the poem's real subject is the woman's disappointment, which the title can name.

title: The final blame
short: Lysander curses everything, but especially Cloris's charms, for damning him to impotence, a conventional excuse the poem exposes.
body: The male speakers of 'imperfect enjoyment' poems typically blame the woman's beauty or their own excess for their failure. Lysander's rage at 'the Shepherdess's Charms' is the standard move, but after the narrator's declared sympathy for Cloris it reads as ironic: the man transfers his shame to the woman. 'Influence' keeps its astrological sense of a power flowing from the stars, so her charms are compared to malignant stars. The religious vocabulary ends in 'Hell'.
